wa_new_millennium_wall.blurb: A small wall in the Shady Hollow group on Mount Erie, near Anacortes, reached by a short walk from the main trail through the woods. It holds around twenty routes, a mix of trad lines and bolted sport climbs, with a single top-rope. The grades lean gentle: a few easy scrambly pitches, a good block of 5.8 and 5.9 climbs, and just one 5.10, so it suits newer leaders and anyone building mileage on moderate terrain. Expect short, friendly lines rather than a big-wall feel. It faces west, which makes it a better bet for late-day sun than for a cold morning start.

wa_west_face_5.blurb: The bolted western side of Big Rock, the central formation of the Rocks of Sharon on Spokane's northeast edge. Most of the twenty routes here are sport climbs of about two pitches, and strong climbers often link them into one long pitch with plenty of draws. Grades cluster from 5.9 up through 5.11, with a handful of easier lines and one aid route, so it is better for solid leaders than for first-timers. The face looks west and has a roof feature. Anchors are set for rappelling back down, and the walk up from the trailhead takes you to the first big rock you meet.

wa_uw_husky_rock.blurb: An outdoor practice wall on the University of Washington campus in Seattle, built in the 1970s from poured concrete with natural stones set in. Five separate walls tilted at different angles give ten climbable sides, topping out around 32 feet, with a gravel bed underneath to soften falls. Nearly all of it is bouldering, from simple jug ladders and easy mantels through mid-grade V3 and V4 problems to a few hard V5 lines, plus a couple of traverses and a top-rope option. It is a convenient city spot for a short session between classes or after work, good for training and for newcomers.

wa_umbrella_rock.blurb: A small, little-visited crag east of Mount Vernon, off Lake Cavanaugh Road near the Walker Valley area. The climbing is on a pair of glacial erratic boulders, with roughly fifteen pitches between them, almost all bolted face climbs. Most are hard, with plenty at 5.11 and 5.12 and a lone 5.13, and only a couple of easier pitches; two short boulder problems sit at the base. Bring about a dozen draws. The stone is sharp and can be loose or flaky in places, and the trail in is faint and overgrown, so this suits experienced climbers who like quiet, scrappy outings.

wa_substation.blurb: The first crag you meet at Exit 38 off I-90, tucked beneath a tall railroad trestle about half an hour east of Seattle. Twenty bolted sport routes run from easy 5.6 and 5.7 climbs up to a handful of 5.11s, with the biggest group at 5.10. The wall is slightly overhanging in the middle, and a damp streak runs down its centre. Tree cover keeps the rock wet for a long time after rain, so pick a dry spell. Belay space is tight in places, and the short, well-worn trail makes it a handy after-work stop.
wa_substation.parking_note: Take I-90 to Exit 38, turn right at the bottom of the ramp and follow SE Homestead Valley Road for roughly half a mile. Leave the car in one of the gravel pullouts on the left, just before the road crosses Change Creek.
wa_substation.approach: A short, well-worn trail climbs through the woods from the road to the railroad trestle, where the wall sits.

wa_rattletale_wall.blurb: A steep, secluded forest cliff in the Lookout Point area above the town of Index, in the Skykomish Valley. Most of the twenty routes are trad, mainly crack lines, with a handful of sport climbs, two aid lines and one boulder problem. The grades are mostly 5.10 and 5.11, with a few easier trad pitches and a couple of much harder lines, so it rewards confident leaders who like cracks and steep granodiorite. Several routes run to multiple pitches. It is a quieter alternative to the main town walls, reached by a trail through the woods and a talus field.

wa_rattlesnake_rock.blurb: A steep crag in Tumwater Canyon along Highway 2, just outside Leavenworth. Of the twenty routes, about two thirds are bolted and the rest are trad. The main sport wall holds mostly 5.11 climbs, with some 5.10 and a few 5.12 lines, on clean, steep rock with small edges. It stays shaded in the morning, which helps on warm days. The walk up is steep and loose with tight switchbacks and rockfall potential for anyone below, so poles help and big groups may prefer elsewhere. A stick clip helps with a few hard starts.
